name: Rongli
tagline: Permit town and old market at the foot of the Silk Route
meta_description: Rongli, Sikkim: sub-division HQ and Silk Route permit town at about 1,585 m. Old trade-route market, distances, jeep fares, ATMs and stays on the way to Zuluk.
summary: Rongli is the headquarters of Rongli sub-division in Pakyong district, on the Rangpo river at about 1,585 m. It is where Indian visitors get the Silk Route protected-area permit before climbing to Padamchen, Zuluk and Nathang. Wikipedia calls it one of the oldest markets of Sikkim, on the old Kalimpong to Tibet trade route.
intro: Rongli is a working market town on National Highway 717B, about 22 km from Pakyong and 62 to 69 km from Gangtok by the figures Wikipedia gives. It lies on the bank of the Rangpo river, where Rongli Khola meets it. Most visitors know it as the permit stop on the way to Zuluk, but it has older roots as a trading place on the Kalimpong to Tibet route.

The permit work is done here. Your driver, agent or homestay takes your documents to the office, and the permit is issued for your names, dates and vehicle. On a good day this takes 30 to 60 minutes; on busy weekends in October it can take two hours. The permit is for Indian nationals only. Foreigners are not allowed beyond Rongli on the Old Silk Route.

The town has a bazaar, banks, ATMs, taxi stands and SNT bus services to Gangtok and Siliguri. Stock up on cash and water here, because the road above has few ATMs. Rongli is rarely a destination for a night, but it is a sensible stop when the permit office closes early. Check current status of permit hours and roads before you travel.

story.title: One of Sikkim's oldest markets
story.text: Wikipedia's article on Rongli says it is one of the oldest markets of Sikkim and lies on the trade route between Kalimpong and Tibet. The article on Jelep La, the pass at the end of that road, describes the Kalimpong route as passing through Rongli, Rhenock and Pedong, and says wool and furs were traded along it in the twentieth century, with Kalimpong as the contact point. Wikipedia's Dzuluk article adds that traders used Zuluk as an overnight base on the route through Pedong, Aritar, Zuluk and Jelep La to the Chumbi valley until about 1959. So Rongli was the lower market and the last big supply stop before the climb. Today the same road is NH 717B, which Wikipedia says runs from Rhenock to Menla near Sherathang via Rongli and Zuluk. The mule trains have gone, but a permit office, a taxi stand and a bazaar still stand where the climb begins.
story.source: Wikipedia: Rongli; Wikipedia: Jelep La; Wikipedia: Dzuluk

little_known.fact: Wikipedia lists the villages around Rongli town as including Rolep, Lingtam, Padamchen, Zuluk, Kupup and Gnathang, so the whole Silk Route falls inside Rongli sub-division.
Wikipedia says SNT buses run from Rongli to Siliguri via Rorathang, Rangpo and Sevoke, and another SNT service connects Rongli to Gangtok via Rorathang, Pakyong and Ranipool.
Two rivers, the Rangpo and the Jaldhaka, originate from lakes in Rongli sub-division, according to Wikipedia. The Rangpo flows past Rorathang to the Teesta; the Jaldhaka flows towards Bhutan.

highlights.title: Silk Route permit office
highlights.text: The protected-area permit for Padamchen, Zuluk, Nathang and Kupup is processed here for Indian nationals. Carry ID and photos for all travellers, and use an agent or homestay to save time.

highlights.title: The old market
highlights.text: Wikipedia calls Rongli one of the oldest markets of Sikkim. Walk the bazaar for tea, groceries and supplies, and ask before photographing people or stalls.

highlights.title: Cash, water and supplies
highlights.text: Banks and ATMs here and at Rhenock are the last dependable ones before the climb. Stock water, snacks and any medicines before leaving.

highlights.title: Transport hub
highlights.text: Shared jeeps run to Gangtok, Pakyong, Rhenock, Rorathang and Rangpo, and SNT buses connect Rongli with Gangtok and Siliguri. Services thin out in the afternoon.

highlights.title: Rivers and waterfalls nearby
highlights.text: Rongli sits where Rongli Khola meets the Rangpo river, and Wikipedia's Aritar article mentions Kali Khola falls on the Rorathang to Rongli road. Both are best in settled weather.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from Gangtok and Rangpo to Rongli through the day, about ₹200–300 a seat from Gangtok and 2.5 to 3.5 hours. SNT buses also run via Rorathang and Pakyong. Services are fewer in the afternoon, so check current status before you travel.
From Gangtok about 65 km and 3 hours via Ranipool, Pakyong and Rorathang. A reserved small car costs about ₹3,500–5,000 one way. In the monsoon, NH10 and side roads can have slides; allow extra time.

About 110 km and 4 to 4.5 hours via Sevoke, Rangpo and Rorathang. If NH10 is shut, the alternative is via Kalimpong, Pedong and Rhenock. Pakyong Airport has no scheduled flights since June 2024, so plan on Bagdogra (IXB) or NJP.

costs: Reserved small car Gangtok to Rongli
where_to_stay: Most travellers do not sleep in Rongli. A few small lodges serve people who arrive after the permit office closes, at roughly ₹1,000–2,000 a room, though quality varies and we do not name them. Better choices are Lingtam homestays just above, Aritar below, or Pakyong's Vivanta for comfort. Padamchen homestays are our usual first night for the high road. If you must stay, ask your driver to book ahead in busy October weeks.
tips: Send ID scans to your homestay a day ahead so the permit waits for you.
Carry original ID and two passport photos for every traveller, children included.
Arrive before about 2 pm because offices can stop issuing in the afternoon.
Withdraw cash here or at Pakyong; ATMs above Rongli are unreliable.
Buy water, snacks and medicines before the climb, and check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Permit morning and bazaar stroll
experiences.summary: A first stop on the Silk Route: get the protected-area permit sorted, then walk the old market for tea, supplies and a feel for the trade road.
body: The permit is issued in your names for specific dates and a specific vehicle, and your driver, agent or homestay carries the documents to the office. Expect 30 to 60 minutes on a normal day. Offices keep government hours and sometimes close on holidays.

While you wait, walk the bazaar. Wikipedia calls Rongli one of the oldest markets in Sikkim on the old trade route to Tibet. Look at the grocery shops, tea stalls, hardware and the taxi stands. Ask before photographing people.

Buy water, snacks, batteries and medicines before going up, and withdraw cash. Keep your permit paper safe and carry copies, because you will be asked for it at check posts. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long does the permit take?
faqs.a: Often 30 to 60 minutes, sometimes two hours in busy weeks. Documents must be complete. Offices keep government hours and may stop issuing in the afternoon. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What do we need for the permit?
faqs.a: Original photo ID for every traveller, photocopies and two passport photos each, children included. The permit is in your names and for your vehicle. Indian nationals only.

faqs.q: Can foreigners get a permit here?
faqs.a: No. The Old Silk Route beyond Rongli is not open to foreigners. Foreign visitors can stay at Aritar or Rhenock and see the lake and bazaars. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Trade-route history walk in Rongli
experiences.image_query: Old trade route Sikkim Tibet mule
experiences.summary: A short self-guided walk with a story: Rongli as the lower market on the Kalimpong to Jelep La trade road, using what Wikipedia and local people can tell you.
body: Wikipedia's article on Jelep La describes the Kalimpong route to the pass as passing through Rongli, Rhenock and Pedong, and says wool and furs were traded along it. The Dzuluk article says trade continued until about 1959.

Walk the main street with that in mind. Ask older shopkeepers, politely and only if they are free, what they remember of the road before the highway. Do not push for stories; many will not have any, and some will not want to talk.

End at a tea stall. Look up the hill road at the start of NH 717B and think of mule trains starting the climb. This is a thinking walk, not a sightseeing one, so bring your imagination and a notebook.

faqs.q: Is there a museum in Rongli?
faqs.a: Not that we know of. The history is in the road, the bazaar and in books. Check current status before you travel. For a wider view, Gangtok has the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology.

faqs.q: What was traded on the old route?
faqs.a: Wikipedia's Jelep La article says wool and furs moved along the Kalimpong route in the twentieth century, with Kalimpong as the contact point. Other goods are mentioned in general histories. We do not claim a full list.

faqs.q: Can we hire a guide for history?
faqs.a: Not formally. Some drivers and homestay hosts know the road's stories. Ask politely. Treat what you hear as told locally unless it is in a book.

experiences.title: Bazaar tea and momo crawl
experiences.summary: A light food walk around Rongli's market: milk tea, momos, noodles and fried snacks from small stalls, to fuel you before the high road.
body: Rongli's food scene is small and honest: tea stalls, momo counters and small thali places serving local office workers, drivers and farmers. Start with tea and a plate of momos.
Try thukpa on a cool day and sel roti if available in season. Eat where it is busy, because turnover is fresh. Ask about ingredients if you avoid meat or eggs.
Carry hand sanitiser and bottled water. Prices are low, so tip small. If you plan to climb the same day, eat lightly, since the road is winding.

faqs.q: Is street food safe in Rongli?
faqs.a: Generally fine at busy stalls with hot, fresh food. Avoid raw salads and ice if your stomach is sensitive. Carry sanitiser and bottled water. Drink hot tea.

faqs.q: Are there vegetarian options?
faqs.a: Yes. Vegetable momos, noodles, thali and fried snacks are easy to find. Say if you avoid onion, garlic or egg. Not every stall separates vegetarian and non-vegetarian cooking.

faqs.q: When are stalls open?
faqs.a: Usually from about 7 am to early evening. Many close earlier on Sundays and holidays. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Rongli river meeting point viewpoint
experiences.summary: A short stop to look at the river where Rongli Khola meets the Rangpo, the water that runs down to Rorathang and Rangpo and joins the Teesta.
body: Wikipedia says Rongli Khola and the Rangpo river meet at Rongli, and the Rangpo then flows on towards Pakyong sub-division, Rorathang and Rangpo town. It is one of the main rivers of east Sikkim.
Ask your driver or a local to point to a safe spot, usually near a bridge or lane above the water. Do not go to the edge, and keep away in or after heavy rain, when rivers rise quickly.
Early morning light is best for photographs. Look for dippers and wagtails on rocks. Do not swim, and keep children away from the bank.

faqs.q: Which rivers meet at Rongli?
faqs.a: Wikipedia says Rongli Khola and the Rangpo river meet at Rongli. The Rangpo then flows on past Rorathang and joins the Teesta at Rangpo town.

faqs.q: Is the river safe to touch or wade?
faqs.a: Not in the main channel. Water can rise fast after upstream rain, and rocks are slippery. Stay on the bank and keep children close.

faqs.q: Is it worth a stop?
faqs.a: Briefly. It is a quiet spot if you have time while a permit is processed. It is not a major sight. Combine it with the bazaar walk.

faqs.q: What is Rongli known for?
faqs.a: Rongli is the headquarters of Rongli sub-division and the permit town for the Old Silk Route. Wikipedia calls it one of the oldest markets of Sikkim, on the trade route between Kalimpong and Tibet. It has a bazaar, banks and taxi stands.

faqs.q: Where do I get the Silk Route permit?
faqs.a: At Rongli, through a registered agent, your driver or your homestay, for Indian nationals only. Carry photo ID and two passport photos for every traveller. The fee is about ₹200–500 per person including handling. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Rongli from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 65 km, taking roughly 3 hours via Ranipool, Pakyong and Rorathang. Wikipedia gives 62 to 69 km depending on the page. Monsoon slides can add time. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM in Rongli?
faqs.a: Yes, there are banks and ATMs, but they can be offline or empty. Withdraw cash before you arrive from Pakyong, Rhenock or Gangtok. Above Rongli, ATMs are rare.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Rongli?
faqs.a: Foreigners with a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit can pass through Rongli, but cannot go beyond on the Old Silk Route, including Zuluk. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long does the permit take?
faqs.a: Usually 30 to 60 minutes, up to two hours on busy weekends. Offices keep government hours, may close on holidays and may stop issuing in the afternoon. Arrange it in advance if your homestay offers.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Rongli?
faqs.a: Yes, small lodges exist at about ₹1,000–2,000 a room, but most travellers prefer Lingtam, Padamchen or Aritar. Ask your driver to book ahead in busy weeks.

faqs.q: How do I get to Rongli by public transport?
faqs.a: Shared jeeps run from Gangtok, Rangpo and Rhenock, and SNT buses connect Rongli with Gangtok and Siliguri via Rorathang. Services thin out in the afternoon. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which airport is nearest to Rongli?
faqs.a: Pakyong Airport is about 24 km away by Wikipedia's figure but has had no scheduled flights since June 2024. Bagdogra (IXB) is about 110 km. NJP is the nearest main railhead. Check current status before you travel.
